html:
Lənape Haki-nk, "Lenape land", or Lenapehoking, was the homeland of the Lenape or Delaware people: today's New Jersey, eastern Pennsylvania, southern New York and northern Delaware, along the Delaware and lower Hudson rivers. The Lenape are an Algonquian people, speaking Munsee in the north and Unami in the south.

They grew maize, beans and squash, fished and hunted, moving between villages with the seasons. Manhattan, a Munsee name, was on their land, and in 1626 the Dutch claimed to buy it. In 1682 William Penn made a treaty of friendship with the Lenape at Shackamaxon. But frauds such as the Walking Purchase of 1737 took their land, and they moved west in stages, to Ohio, Indiana, Kansas and finally Oklahoma and Ontario.

The English named the Delaware River after an English lord, Baron De La Warr, and then called the Lenape after the river. See also Delaware and Munsee Lenape.
